newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Delco Electronics fights to keep market lead. [CORRECTED 08:26 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Delco Electronics fights to keep market lead. [CORRECTED 08:26 GMT]

text.p: U.S. automotive electronics company Delco Electronics Corp is fighting to keep its lead in market share in the face of intense competition, vice president William Spelman said on Thursday.
"The industry is growing at a 20 percent annual rate. We intend to maintain our lead position," he told reporters, adding that the company had a 23 percent world market share.

"In so doing we have to be more than two times larger...more than US$10 billion by the year 2000," (corrects to add reference to the year 2000) he said after receiving the Operational Headquarters Award for Delco in Singapore, which brings the company some tax breaks.

Delco Electronics is part of Hughes Electronics Corp, a unit of General Motors Corp and a huge part of its production is sold to to U.S. automobile giant. Delco reported revenue of US$5.6 billion in 1995.
A Delco statement said the market for automotive electronics was worth more than US$25 billion and was expected to approach US$40 billion within the next 10 years.
Spelman, who is also president of Delco Electronics Asia Pacific, said the company was facing pressure on its operating margin and was working hard to raise it back to the 15 percent level.

"Competition is tremendous. The 15 percent is obviously something that we want. We have the expertise to improve ...we invest in our growth and on technology to be able to maintain that position. We do not intend to relinquish that," he said.

Analysts said Delco's margins were being squeezed in recent years, mainly due to General Motors' demand for price cuts in its automotive operations. Delco Electronics operating margin is projected at 13 percent in 1996.
Spelman said more than 20 percent of Delco's worldwide customers were now outside General Motors and the company was looking to raise this portion of business.
The Asia Pacific region was key to the company's growth and it expected sales to more than double by 2000, he said.
Rob Leggat, director of public affairs and administration, said Delco's sales to Asia Pacific customers were more than US$200 million in 1995.

Spelman said Delco was investing in manufacturing technology, working on cost competitiveness and various forms of partnership, including joint ventures in the Asia Pacific. It has seven joint ventures in the region, including two manufacturing joint ventures in China.

Delco is investing US$50 million over the next three years in microelectronics technology in Singapore for its automative sensor and safety products. To date it had invested US$150 million in Singapore, Leggat said.

It launched the initial phase of a side-impact smart sensor production line at its Singapore plant on Thursday. When a car is hit from the side, the sensor instantly triggers the air bag. More than five million sensors will be produced from Singapore yearly for customers worldwide.

Sales from its Singapore plant were S$490 million (US$350 million) in 1995, said Jimmy Quah, managing director of Delco Electronics Singapore Pte Ltd, and growth is expected to be flat in 1996 due to strikes in the United States.
